judgement_by: Hon. Dr. D. F. H. Gunawardhana, J.
keywords: The Petitioner’s husband was the former Senior DSG who assisted and advised the Anti-Corruption Committee set up by the Yahapalana Government between 2015 to 2019. The President of the successive Government of 2020 appointed a Commission of Inquiry in terms of Act No. 17 of 1948 to inquire into allegations of political victimisation during the Yahapalana regime; on a complaint made by a person who had been indicted before the High Court on the findings of the Anti-Corruption Committee where the Petitioner’s husband had acted as the advisor on the secondment and later was the prosecutor before the High Court, the Commission inquired into the allegations and made certain recommendations without his participation. Held – the Mandate did not permit the Commissioners to look into the said matter, and they had flouted the rules of natural justice; Petitioner’s husband had acted according to law and within the parameters as a lawyer attached to the Attorney General’s Department; writs issued.
legistation: The Constitution of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

keywords: The Petitioner challenged the direction contained in the notification sent by the UDA for the service charges of a conversion of a residential property to a business premises. According to the UDA, the said charges were imposed based on the Regulations promulgated according to the relevant Acts and depending on the square foot area of the premises in suit. Therefore, without challenging the said regulations, the Petitioner cannot challenge the said direction of the notification. Held – the Petitioner is liable to pay the said charges if his application is for the said conversion which the UDA officials found the entire premises to have been converted into a business premises despite the Petitioner’s claim that only a part of the premises is to be converted into a business premises. Application dismissed.

keywords: The original grantee died and his wife had not succeeded within six months of his death; she had sold her rights to a third party. In the meantime, the 4 th Respondent, the next of kin in the line of succession (the original grantee’s eldest son), was convicted for a triple murder which was later affirmed by the Supreme Court. Therefore, certain functionaries under the Land Development Ordinance, in the belief that he had lost his civil rights, pending the execution of his capital punishment imposed upon him, had decided to accept his younger brother as the next of kin and successor, and accordingly took steps to register his name erroneously. Thereafter, he has transferred his rights to the present Petitioner. The 4th Respondent made an application to succeed. On the advice of the Attorney General, the Commissioner General of Lands directed the 3rd Respondent (Divisional Secretary) to accept the 4th Respondent as the successor; the Petitioner challenged the same. Held – Application dismissed; the Attorney General’s advice is the correct; at certain times, certain functionaries under the Land Development Ordinance, having misread and misinterpreted the legal provisions, had misapplied them.
legistation: The Constitution of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

On the advice of the Attorney General, the Commissioner General of Lands directed the 3rd Respondent (Divisional Secretary) to accept the 4th Respondent as the successor; the Petitioner challenged the same. Held – Application dismissed; the Attorney General’s advice is the correct; at certain times, certain functionaries under the Land Development Ordinance, having misread and misinterpreted the legal provisions, had misapplied them.

keywords: The Petitioner claims that his uncle (3rd Respondent) failed to succeed to the rights as a successor of his late grandfather, who had been the original grantee of a parcel of land given under the Land Development Ordinance. However, the Respondents’ stand is that the 3rd Respondent could not have succeeded after the death of the original grantee in 1996 until the death of the spouse of the original grantee (mother of the 3rd Respondent) in terms of Section 48B. The question of succession arose thereafter in 2022, and the 3rd Respondent has duly applied to register his succession which had been nominated by the original grantee under the original permit issued prior to the grant. Held – acceptance of the 3rd Respondent as the successor by the Divisional Secretary on the instructions of the Commissioner General of Land is valid, and therefore, the registration in the Land Registry of the 3rd Respondent as the successor to the original grantee is valid; Application dismissed.

keywords: The Petitioner claims that his uncle (3rd Respondent) failed to succeed to the rights as a successor of his late grandfather, who had been the original grantee of a parcel of land given under the Land Development Ordinance. However, the Respondents’ stand is that the 3rd Respondent could not have succeeded after the death of the original grantee in 1996 until the death of the spouse of the original grantee (mother of the 3rd Respondent) in terms of Section 48B. The question of succession arose thereafter in 2022, and the 3rd Respondent has duly applied to register his succession which had been nominated by the original grantee under the original permit issued prior to the grant. Held – acceptance of the 3rd Respondent as the successor by the Divisional Secretary on the instructions of the Commissioner General of Land is valid, and therefore, the registration in the Land Registry of the 3rd Respondent as the successor to the original grantee is valid; Application dismissed.

keywords: The Petitioner, a Society running a religious institute and Hindu Temple, was occupying a land within the vicinity of the Sri Maha Bodhi in the sacred city of Anuradhapura. Later, with the dawn of the Buddha Jayanthi era of 1956, the Petitioner was relocated by giving a land, where the Petitioner also ran a school which was vested in the Government under the Assisted Schools and Training Colleges Act. Thereafter, the Petitioner was placed in possession of another land, where it operated a religious institute including a Temple, cultural centre, and restaurant. The excess land was blocked out and given to the 8th to 10th Respondents. Dispute arose between them with regard to the regularisation and legalisation of their possession by the Government on the recommendation of the Provincial Land Commissioner, which the Petitioner objected to. Held - Application dismissed on the basis that the Petitioner has no legal title to claim nor any legitimate expectation to claim any title document since the Petitioner has failed to improve or develop the entire land; the Petitioner is not entitled to benefit out of his own fault.

judgement_by: Ho.n.Dr. D. F. H. Gunawardhana, J.
keywords: The Petitioner was involved in two robberies while serving as a police officer. Though he was acquitted from criminal proceedings, he was charge-sheeted by a disciplinary panel appointed by the Senior DIG of the range to which he was attached. Panel of Inquiry found him guilty on the strong evidence against him; findings against him by the Panel of Inquiry was further affirmed by the Public Service Commission and Administrative Appeal Tribunal. However, on sympathetic grounds he was permitted to retire. The Petitioner challenges the vires of the appointment of Panel of Inquiry and its findings. Held – the Petitioner, being a Sub- Inspector, is subject to the disciplinary control of the Senior DIG of the range to which he is attached, therefore, the appointment is intra vires and based on the facts, the final findings of the AAT is justified; thus, Application dismissed.
legistation: The Constitution of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

keywords: The Petitioner, being the importer on record registered under Section 115 of the Customs Ordinance, had imported certain consignment of goods, part of which was not declared in the Customs Declaration form. It was investigated into since there was a mismatch between the Customs Declaration and the Bill of Lading and the packing list. After inquiry, the goods were ordered to be released on payment of Custom duty and certain penalty. Subsequently, the producing officer made an application to the Director General to revise the order and sought a direction under Section 2 read with Section 47 as well. After full-scale inquiry, penalty was imposed under Section 47; Petitioner challenges the same. Held – the Respondents’ actions are legal and justifiable, and the order made under Section 47 is justifiable as well.

keywords: The Petitioner being the eldest child of the original permit holder, who had died and nominated his wife as the successor, sought to be substituted. The same permit holder held two plots of land, one on permit issued under the Land Development Ordinance, and the other one’s permit was on the pipeline to be issued. The widow never made an application to succeed within the time stipulated as she had also died within sixteen months of the death of the original permit holder. The Divisional Secretary decided to amalgamate both lands and divided into equal shares among all the children. The Petitioner successfully invoked the jurisdiction of this Court to obtain a Writ of Certiorari and Mandamus to declare him as the successor in respect of the plot of land held under permit.
legistation: The Constitution of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

description: Neshakumaran Vimalaraj Vs The University Grants Commission and Others before Hon.Dr. D. F. H. Gunawardhana, J.
parties: Neshakumaran Vimalaraj Vs The University Grants Commission and Others
judgement_by: Hon.Dr. D. F. H. Gunawardhana, J.
keywords: The Petitioner was a Council Member of the Eastern University for a period of three years. After the present Government came into power, the members of the University Grants Commission were newly appointed and they requested the Petitioner to resign from his said post; on refusal, he was removed. The said decision was challenged by way of writ. The main defense taken up by the Respondents was that the Petitioner was removed in implementing National policy. However, the National policy that was relied upon was the election manifesto of a political party. Held – no election manifesto can be accepted or adopted as National policy if it is violative of the law and Constitution, unless the law and Constitution are changed. Writ of Certiorari and Mandamus was issued.
legistation: The Constitution of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

judgement_by: Hon.Dr. D. F. H. Gunawardhana, J.
keywords: The Petitioner was a Council Member of the Eastern University for a period of three years. After the present Government came into power, the members of the University Grants Commission were newly appointed and they requested the Petitioner to resign from his said post; on refusal, he was removed. The said decision was challenged by way of writ. The main defense taken up by the Respondents was that the Petitioner was removed in implementing National policy. However, the National policy that was relied upon was the election manifesto of a political party. Held – no election manifesto can be accepted or adopted as National policy if it is violative of the law and Constitution, unless the law and Constitution are changed. Writ of Certiorari and Mandamus was issued.
legistation: The Constitution of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

judgement_by: Hon. Dr. D. F. H. Gunawardhana, J.
keywords: Partition action instituted in the District Court of Tangalle in respect of land situated within the same jurisdiction. Allegations that the entire land has not been depicted in the preliminary plan. However, before the commencement of the trial, the Petitioner sought the intervention of the writ court to obtain a writ compelling the District Court Judge to dismiss the action for the want of proper identification of the corpus. Held – the writ court cannot intervene into the matter since it affects the Judicial power of the parties since only the District Court of Tangalle has the jurisdiction in terms of Section 3(2) of the Partition Law, Section 6 of the Civil Procedure Code, and the Constitution. Though the writ court is empowered to issue writs, when there is no allegation of irrationality, act of ultra vires affecting the rights of the parties, or acted without evidence, no writ lies.
legistation: The Constitution of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka

keywords: The Petitioners, have invoked the jurisdiction of this court, to seek a mandate in the nature of writ of mandamus to compel the Respondents to remove all unauthorized obstructions in the proposed roadway on Vimukthi Mawatha, Stage II, Anuradhapura, and to compel the said Respondents to demarcate the proposed roadway marked \"H\" in plan No. AalNPE/2012/618-619, marked X6, (hereinafter sometimes referred to as the \"alternative plan\"). The Petitioner has also sought a mandate in the nature of writ of Mandamus to compel the 3rd and 4th Respondents to hold a Land Kachcheri in terms of Section 20, of the Land Development Ordinance. .. 3 The Petitioners submit that after receiving notice in terms of Section 42A, of the Municipal Councils Ordinance, several parties including the 5th Respondent, failed to demolish unauthorized structures obstructing the proposed roadway and the 1 st and! or 2nd Respondents have failed to take necessary steps to have the said unauthorized structures demolished in terms of the said Act. After several failed attempts by the Petitioners to resolve this issue, the 2nd Respondent by letter dated 20104/2012, marked X5(b), has notified the 2nd Petitioner that the matter would be resolved by an alternative plan, as proposed by the Urban Development Authority, (UDA). The said alternative plan drawn and proposed by the UDA has been approved by the planning committee of the 1 st Respondent. By letter dated 10/09/2013, marked X7(b), the 2nd Respondent has approved the said plan for implementation. As pleaded in paragraph 22, the Petitioners through their Attorney-at - Law has made a demand from the 2nd Respondent by letters of demand marked XII and X12, to effectuate the said plan forthwith. However, it is observed that, the 1st Respondent by letter dated 10/09/2013, has informed the said Attorney -at- Law, that the Municipal Council Anuradhapura would take appropriate steps to demolish the unauthorized structures, once the Urban Development Authority submits the alternative plan. Presently, the alternative plan is with the planning committee, of the 1 st Respondent, pending approval. · 4 The Respondents raised a preliminary objection to this application, on the basis that the Petitioners have failed to add the necessary parties to this Petition and therefore, the action should be dismissed in limine. In the case of Wijeratne Vs. Ven Dr. Paragoda Wimalawansa Thero and others, (2011) 2 SLR 258, the Supreme Court considered the effect of necessary parties to an application, where the court held, that; \"those who would be affected by the outcome of the writ application should be made respondents to the application\" In paragraph 4, the petitioner admits that there were several disputes between the residents of Vimukthi Mawatha, Stage II, Anuradhapura, in relation to the road reservation and the unauthorized constructions on the said road reservation. The 5th Respondent is one of the residents of Vimukthi Mawatha, Stage II. According to the pleadings of the Petitioner, it is observed that including the 5 th Respondent there are several other residents who are obstructing the demolition of the unauthorized structures on the proposed roadway. This is observed in the 3rd paragraph of letter dated 31110/2013, written by the 3rd Respondent to the 4th Respondent marked X8. Therefore, the relief sought by the Petitioners would not only affect the 5 th Respondent, but several other residents of Vimukthi Mawatha, Stage II, who are not before Court. The Petitioner has identified only the 5 th Respondent as a resident who was served with a notice in terms of Section 42A, of the Municipal Councils Ordinance. Failure to identify all 5 necessary parties, will not only leave the dispute unresolved but also create multiple avenues of litigation from affected parties. However, it is important at this stage to consider whether, the Petitioners have a legal right to compel the Respondents to clear all obstructions from the roadway, according to plan marked X6, in terms of the relevant statutory provISIOns. It is an admitted fact that the Petitioners, the 5th Respondent and all other parties in possession of allotments of land in Vimukthi Mawatha, occupy allotments of land, unlawfully. As pleaded in paragraph 3 of the Petition, subsequent to an inquiry held by the 3rd Respondent in terms of the Land Development Ordinance No. 19 of 1935 (as amended), the Petitioner and several other parties have been considered to be given permits in terms of Section 19 of the said Act. However, as of now, no permits under the said Act have been issued to any of the parties. The Petitioners submit that, the disputes between residents of Viniukthi Mawatha regarding the road reservation and unauthorized constructions have not been referred to a land Kachcheri under the Land Development Ordinance. It is observed that, by this application the Petitioners are not challenging the non-granting of the permits to the said lands nor have the Petitioners placed on record any supporting evidence for the Court to make any direction to hold a Land Kachcheri to sought out the issue of land allotments. 6 The Petitioners are seeking to compel the relevant Authorities to remove unauthorized obstructions in order to proceed with the proposed roadway. However, in the absence of a clear legal right to occupy the land allotments, the Petitioner cannot compel the authorities to perform a specific statutory duty to demolish the said unauthorized structures. It is observed, that the Petitioners have no clear legal right to compel the 1 st and 2nd Respondents, to remove unauthorized structures obstructing the roadway, since the Petitioners are not in lawful possession of the said allotments of land. Their rights, if any, would be decided upon the awarding of a permit, in terms of the Land Development Ordinance. Therefore, there is no legal duty thrust upon the 1 st and the 2nd Respondents to remove unauthorized obstructions on the proposed roadway. However, the 1 st and 2nd Respondents are directed to speedily resolve the issue of demolition of the unauthorized structures in Vimukthi Mawatha, Stage II according to the Law. It is noted that in spite of the undertaking given to court, the Petitioners have failed to file written submissions in support of this application. In the circumstances, the Petition is dismissed without costs.

keywords: Partition action involving land transferred by parents to six children. Defendant claimed prescriptive title through exclusive possession, relying on an informal letter from a co-owner as proof of ouster. Court held the letter amounted only to an agreement to sell, not a valid transfer, and that the defendant had always possessed it as a co-owner. Defendant\'s claim to exclude other co-owners failed. Appeal dismissed.

keywords: The 10th Defendant-Appellant sought re-listing of an appeal rejected in 1997 after non-appearance.
